Aguijjim is monkfish and bean sprouts braised together in a thick garlicky chili sauce meant for sharing. It's very spicy so pace yourself. Everyone eats from the middle of the table. Use your chopsticks to pick out the fish and sprouts. It has fish and soy in it so it's out if you avoid seafood. This is general info, not medical advice. Check with the restaurant about allergies.

Bulgogi is thin slices of beef marinated in sweet soy sauce with garlic and sesame oil, then grilled until tender. There is no heat to it at all. It's sweet and savory. Eat it straight with rice or wrap a piece in lettuce with garlic. It has soy and sesame in it, and the soy sauce may bring gluten. This is general info, not medical advice. Check with the restaurant about allergies.

Kimchi jjigae is a bubbling stew of aged kimchi, pork, tofu, and a tangy broth. The kimchi and chili flakes give it a solid kick. It comes in a shared pot, so ladle some into your own bowl and eat it with rice. It has soy in it, the broth sometimes has fish or seafood, and the pork version isn't halal or kosher. This is general info, not medical advice. Check with a restaurant about allergies.

Samgyeopsal is thick slices of plain pork belly that you grill yourself at the table. The meat isn't spicy, though the dipping paste that comes with it is. Wrap a slice in a lettuce leaf with garlic and a dab of that paste. It has soy in it and it's pork, so skip it if you avoid either. This is general info, not medical advice. Check with the restaurant about allergies.

Galbitang is beef short ribs simmered slowly into a clear soup with radish and glass noodles. There's no heat at all, just a light, savory broth seasoned with salt and garlic. Pull the tender meat off the ribs with your spoon and sip the broth as you go. It's mostly free of common allergens, but the soy sauce is worth asking about. This is general info, not medical advice.
